html:
In 1913 the Americans closed the gates of the Gatun Dam across the Chagres River in Panama. Over the next months, water covered the valley behind it and made Gatun Lake, then the largest man-made lake in the world.

The lake was the heart of the Panama Canal. Instead of digging down to sea level, as the French had tried, engineers raised ships up through locks to the lake, which let them cross the middle of the isthmus on water, and cut the digging needed. The plan was backed by the chief engineer John Stevens.

The cost fell on people who lived there. Towns and villages along the Chagres, and the old route of the Panama Railroad, were cleared or moved, and thousands of people lost homes and farms. Some of the line and its stations went under. Treetops and drowned forest stood in the water for years.

The canal opened in 1914. The lake still supplies the locks and much of the drinking water for Panama City, and it is why the canal depends on rainfall.
